title: Skin Pathogens
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Skin is a dry, salty, lipid-coated, constantly shedding surface, so the organisms that cause disease there are the ones equipped to hold on, digest keratin, hide inside cells, or arrive by injection from an arthropod. This chapter covers the bacteria (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Cutibacterium acnes, Pseudomonas aeruginosa), the superficial fungi (dermatophytes, Malassezia, Candida albicans), the DNA viruses (human papillomavirus, molluscum contagiosum, the herpesviruses), and the vector-borne infections that announce themselves on the skin. Board questions give a Gram stain, a culture reaction, a smear, or an exposure history and expect you to name the organism and explain how one virulence factor produces the lesion.
prerequisites: Structure of the epidermis, stratum corneum, hair follicle, and sebaceous gland (IN-1, IN-2)
Innate skin defenses: barrier lipids, acidic pH, antimicrobial peptides, resident flora (IN-10)
Gram stain, catalase, coagulase, hemolysis, and oxidase as identification tests
Neutrophil recruitment, opsonization by IgG and C3b, and complement activation
T cell subsets, especially Th17 and IL-17, and the consequences of neutropenia

connections.how: Keratinocyte Toll-like receptors and Langerhans cells start the inflammatory response that turns colonization into visible disease.
Nephritogenic group A streptococcal skin infection seeds immune complex glomerulonephritis, which is the renal consequence of a skin event.
The site of a Candida infection reports the defect: Th17 and IL-17 pathway failure gives mucocutaneous disease, neutropenia gives invasive disease.
High-risk HPV removes p53 and Rb control through E6 and E7, which is the classic viral route to squamous carcinoma.
Herpesvirus latency in sensory ganglia is why recurrent lesions map onto a dermatome or a single cranial nerve territory.

sections.title: Staphylococcus aureus: identification, virulence factors, and methicillin resistance

blocks.text: Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive coccus that divides in several planes, so it appears in grape-like clusters. It is a facultative anaerobe, catalase positive (which separates all staphylococci from streptococci), and coagulase positive, which separates it from the coagulase-negative skin residents such as Staphylococcus epidermidis. It is salt tolerant, grows on mannitol salt agar with a yellow halo from mannitol fermentation, and is beta-hemolytic. About 30% of people carry it in the anterior nares, which is the usual reservoir for later skin infection.

Each virulence factor defeats one defense, and the lesion follows from which factors are expressed. Coagulase activates prothrombin so that fibrinogen is converted to fibrin, which coats the organism and contributes to the fibrin wall of an abscess; this is why staphylococcal infection is typically localized and purulent rather than spreading. Protein A binds the Fc portion of IgG, so bound antibody faces outward in the wrong orientation and can neither be recognized by the neutrophil Fc receptor nor activate the classical complement pathway. Panton-Valentine leukocidin assembles pores in the membranes of neutrophils and macrophages and lyses them, which accounts for the extensive necrosis of community-associated methicillin-resistant abscesses and necrotizing pneumonia. Catalase degrades hydrogen peroxide, blunting the neutrophil oxidative burst.

Two exotoxins act at a distance from the organism and produce syndromes that look nothing like an abscess. Exfoliative toxins A and B are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein 1, the desmosomal cadherin holding granular layer keratinocytes together, so the epidermis splits high within itself and separates without inflammation or mucosal involvement: this is bullous impetigo when local and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome when the toxin is blood-borne. Toxic shock syndrome toxin 1 is a superantigen that bridges MHC class II to the variable beta region of the T cell receptor, bypassing antigen processing and activating up to 20% of T cells at once, with massive interleukin-2, interferon gamma, and tumor necrosis factor release causing fever, rash, and capillary leak with shock.

blocks.text: Methicillin resistance is a change in the drug target rather than drug destruction. Beta-lactams work by acylating the active site serine of penicillin-binding proteins, the transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan. The mecA gene, carried on a mobile staphylococcal cassette chromosome, encodes PBP2a, an alternative transpeptidase whose active site has very low affinity for beta-lactams. When ordinary penicillin-binding proteins are inhibited, PBP2a continues cross-linking the cell wall, so the organism keeps growing and every standard beta-lactam fails, including nafcillin and the cephalosporins that target the usual proteins. This is a different mechanism from penicillinase, the beta-lactamase that hydrolyzes the beta-lactam ring and that nafcillin resists by steric hindrance.

blocks.predict: A child has flaccid bullae that shear off with light pressure, no mucosal lesions, and sterile blister fluid. Which S aureus factor explains all three findings?
blocks.explain: Exfoliative toxin. It is blood-borne, so the organism is not in the blister, it cleaves desmoglein 1 within the granular layer, so the split is superficial and the roof shears off, and desmoglein 1 is not the dominant adhesion molecule in mucosa, so mucous membranes are spared.

sections.title: Streptococcus pyogenes: identification, virulence, and why skin infection causes nephritis but not rheumatic fever

blocks.text: Streptococcus pyogenes, group A Streptococcus, is a gram-positive coccus in chains and is catalase negative, which separates it from the staphylococci. On blood agar it is beta-hemolytic, producing complete clearing from hemolysins. Among beta-hemolytic streptococci it is bacitracin sensitive and PYR positive (it produces the enzyme pyrrolidonyl arylamidase), while group B Streptococcus is bacitracin resistant and hippurate positive with a positive CAMP test. Grouping rests on the Lancefield carbohydrate in the cell wall, and typing on the M protein.

Where S aureus walls itself off, S pyogenes spreads, and its virulence factors explain that difference. M protein, a surface fibrillar protein, binds the complement regulator factor H, which accelerates C3b breakdown on the bacterial surface, so opsonization and phagocytosis fail. The hyaluronic acid capsule is chemically the same polymer as host connective tissue ground substance, so it is poorly immunogenic and resists engulfment. Streptokinase converts plasminogen to plasmin, which lyses the fibrin that would otherwise contain the organism, and hyaluronidase and DNases loosen ground substance and liquefy the viscous DNA of lysed neutrophils. Together these let infection advance along fascial planes and dermal lymphatics, which is why erysipelas and cellulitis spread diffusely with lymphangitic streaking rather than forming a single abscess. Streptolysin O is an oxygen-labile, cholesterol-dependent pore-forming cytolysin and is strongly immunogenic, so the antistreptolysin O titer documents recent infection; streptolysin S is oxygen stable and responsible for surface hemolysis but is not immunogenic. Pyrogenic exotoxins A and C are superantigens, giving the sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue of scarlet fever and, with deeper invasion, streptococcal toxic shock.

The two major postinfectious syndromes follow different mechanisms, and that difference is the reason skin infection can cause one but not the other. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is immune complex disease: antibody binds nephritogenic streptococcal antigens, complexes accumulate on the subepithelial side of the glomerular capillary wall as the subepithelial humps seen on electron microscopy, complement is activated, and a nephritic picture of hematuria, periorbital edema, hypertension, and low serum C3 appears about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis or about 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo. The antigens involved belong to strains that cause either pharyngitis or impetigo, so the skin route works. Acute rheumatic fever instead depends on molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells raised against M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin, laminin, and valve glycoproteins, and only a limited set of rheumatogenic M types, carried in the throat rather than on skin, elicit that response. The prevailing explanation is that the pharyngeal lymphoid tissue generates the systemic antibody and T cell response needed, while skin strains differ in M type and provoke a weaker systemic response, so pyoderma is followed by nephritis but not carditis.

sections.title: Dermatophytes and Malassezia: fungi that live in keratin and sebum

blocks.text: Dermatophytes are keratinophilic molds in three genera: Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton. They secrete keratinases, mostly subtilisin-like and fungalysin proteases, that cleave the disulfide-rich keratin of cornified tissue into peptides the fungus can absorb. Because their nutrient source is dead keratin and they are restricted by temperature and by serum inhibitory factors, they grow in the stratum corneum, hair shaft, and nail plate and do not invade living epidermis or dermis in an immunocompetent host. The visible lesion is therefore produced partly by the fungus and largely by the host: hyphae advance outward from the point of inoculation while the immune response and resulting inflammation are strongest at the advancing margin, giving the annular scaly plaque with a raised active border and a clearing center that is called tinea or ringworm.

Diagnosis rests on microscopy of scale, nail, or hair in 10% to 20% potassium hydroxide, which dissolves keratinocytes and leaves the alkali-resistant fungal wall visible. Dermatophytes show long, branching, septate hyphae, often with arthroconidia. Site names describe location rather than organism: tinea capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, and unguium. The genera differ in which keratinized tissues they invade, a distinction that is commonly tested.

blocks.title: Dermatophyte genera and tissues invaded
blocks.caption: Trichophyton invades all three; Microsporum spares nail and Epidermophyton spares hair.

blocks.text: Malassezia is a different organism with a different niche and must not be grouped with the dermatophytes despite the name tinea versicolor. It is a lipophilic, lipid-dependent budding yeast that lacks the enzymes for fatty acid synthesis, so it requires exogenous lipid and lives as normal flora in sebum-rich skin of the upper trunk, shoulders, neck, and face. Overgrowth under heat, humidity, occlusion, or high sebum output produces well-demarcated macules that release fine scale when scraped and that may fluoresce yellow-green under a Wood lamp. The scrape in potassium hydroxide shows the characteristic combination of short, blunt, sometimes angular hyphal fragments mixed with clusters of round budding yeast cells, the appearance described as spaghetti and meatballs, which is distinct from the long branching septate hyphae of a dermatophyte.

The pigment change explains the word versicolor. Malassezia produces dicarboxylic acids, including azelaic acid, that competitively inhibit tyrosinase in neighboring melanocytes, so melanin synthesis in the involved skin falls and lesions appear hypopigmented, a difference that becomes obvious when surrounding skin tans. In other patients, or on other body sites and skin tones, lesions appear hyperpigmented, attributed to a thickened keratin layer, larger melanosomes, and the inflammatory response rather than to reduced melanin. Malassezia also contributes to Pityrosporum folliculitis and to seborrheic dermatitis, where lipase-released free fatty acids irritate the follicular and scalp epithelium.

sections.title: Candida albicans: commensal to pathogen, and what the site of disease reveals about immunity

blocks.text: Candida albicans is a commensal yeast of the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and vagina that becomes a pathogen when local conditions or host defenses change. It is often described as dimorphic because it switches reversibly between forms depending on temperature, pH, carbon dioxide, and nutrients: a round or oval budding yeast at lower temperature, and elongated pseudohyphae and true hyphae at 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit) in serum or tissue. This switch matters because the yeast form is suited to adherence and dissemination while the filamentous form provides the mechanical thrust and the secreted aspartyl proteases and candidalysin that penetrate epithelium. In the laboratory, Candida albicans forms true germ tubes within a few hours in serum at 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and produces thick-walled terminal chlamydoconidia (chlamydospores) on cornmeal agar, both of which separate it from most other Candida species. In tissue or a potassium hydroxide preparation, budding yeasts together with pseudohyphae showing constrictions at the septa identify it.

The mucosal and cutaneous surface is defended in layers. Intact keratinized epithelium, an acidic surface, and a competing bacterial flora that occupies adherence sites and consumes nutrients hold the organism at low density. Above that, epithelial cells recognize fungal cell wall mannan and beta-glucan through C-type lectin receptors, principally dectin-1, signaling through the adaptor CARD9 to drive a Th17 response; interleukin-17 and interleukin-22 then recruit neutrophils to the epithelium and induce antimicrobial peptides and epithelial repair. Within tissue and blood, neutrophils are the decisive effector, killing hyphae by oxidative burst and by releasing neutrophil extracellular traps. Each predisposing factor removes one of these layers, so the pattern of disease identifies which layer failed.

blocks.title: Reading the immune defect from the site
blocks.text: Two patients grow Candida albicans. The first, a young adult with thickened dystrophic nails and persistent oral and esophageal plaques since childhood but no bloodstream infection, has lost IL-17-dependent epithelial defense, so the fungus is never cleared from surfaces, yet neutrophils still prevent invasion. The second, receiving chemotherapy with a neutrophil count of 0.2 times 10 to the 9th per liter and a central line, develops fever and candidemia with scattered papules and retinal lesions. Surface defense is intact, but with no neutrophils in tissue the hyphal form penetrates and disseminates. Surface disease points to the Th17 axis; invasive disease points to neutrophils.

sections.title: Human papillomavirus and molluscum contagiosum: two DNA viruses with opposite strategies

blocks.text: Human papillomavirus is a small nonenveloped virus with a circular double-stranded DNA genome of about 8 kilobases in an icosahedral capsid. Lacking an envelope, it is stable on surfaces and resistant to drying and detergents, which is why transmission works by direct skin contact, autoinoculation from scratching or shaving, fomites such as shower floors, and sexual contact. It enters basal keratinocytes through microabrasions, because only the basal layer still divides and can maintain the genome as a low-copy episome. Its replication is then tied to differentiation: as the infected cell moves upward and keratinizes, viral promoters switch on, the genome amplifies, capsid proteins L1 and L2 are made, and complete virions are assembled in the upper layers and shed with the cornified cells. The cytopathic signature of that late replication is the koilocyte, a superficial keratinocyte with a shrunken wrinkled nucleus and a clear perinuclear halo, accompanied by hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis, which together make the verrucous surface of a wart.

Oncogenic potential separates the low-risk types (1, 2, and 4 on skin; 6 and 11 in anogenital sites) from the high-risk mucosal types (16 and 18 most importantly). In low-risk infection the genome stays episomal and the regulatory protein E2 restrains E6 and E7 expression, so the lesion is a benign, self-limited proliferation. In high-risk infection the genome may integrate into host DNA, and integration commonly disrupts the E2 open reading frame, releasing E6 and E7 from control. E6 recruits the cellular ubiquitin ligase E6AP to direct p53 for proteasomal degradation, removing the G1 damage checkpoint and p53-dependent apoptosis, and E7 binds Rb and displaces it from E2F, which frees E2F to drive S phase entry. The cell divides with unrepaired damage, mutations accumulate, and progression through dysplasia to squamous cell carcinoma becomes possible over years.

blocks.caption: Loss of both the checkpoint and the brake is what makes integration, not infection alone, the oncogenic event.

blocks.text: Molluscum contagiosum virus takes the opposite approach on nearly every point. It is a poxvirus: large, brick-shaped, enveloped, with a linear double-stranded DNA genome, and it carries its own DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and transcription machinery, so unlike other DNA viruses of the skin it replicates entirely in the cytoplasm and never requires the nucleus. Infected keratinocytes enlarge and accumulate assembled virus as large eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions, the molluscum bodies (Henderson-Patterson bodies), and the lesion is a firm, dome-shaped, umbilicated papule whose central plug is composed of those infected cells. The virus encodes multiple immune evasion proteins, including inhibitors of chemokine and interleukin signaling and of apoptosis, which is why lesions are strikingly free of surrounding inflammation and may persist for months before cell-mediated immunity clears them. Spread is by direct skin contact, fomites, and autoinoculation, with sexual transmission in adults; extensive or facial lesions in an adult suggest impaired cellular immunity.

sections.title: Herpes simplex and varicella zoster: epithelial infection, ganglionic latency, and reactivation

blocks.text: Herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 and varicella zoster virus are alphaherpesviruses: enveloped, with linear double-stranded DNA in an icosahedral capsid surrounded by a protein tegument. Envelope glycoproteins attach to heparan sulfate and then to an entry receptor (nectin-1 for herpes simplex), the envelope fuses with the plasma membrane, and the genome enters the nucleus and circularizes, where lytic genes are expressed in an ordered immediate early, early, late cascade. Replication in epithelium causes ballooning degeneration of keratinocytes, fusion into multinucleated giant cells, and intranuclear Cowdry type A inclusions; the resulting intraepidermal edema and cell lysis produce a thin-walled vesicle on an erythematous base that ruptures easily into a shallow painful erosion. A Giemsa- or Wright-stained scraping from the base of a fresh vesicle, the Tzanck smear, shows those giant cells, but it cannot distinguish herpes simplex from varicella zoster, since both fuse cells by the same glycoprotein mechanism.

During the primary infection the virus also enters the unmyelinated terminals of sensory neurons in the skin or mucosa and travels by retrograde axonal transport, using dynein along microtubules, to the neuronal cell body in a sensory ganglion. There the lytic program shuts down, the genome persists as a circular episome, and transcription is limited largely to latency-associated transcripts that suppress apoptosis and lytic gene expression. Because almost no viral protein is made, the neuron presents little antigen on MHC class I, so cytotoxic T cells cannot clear the reservoir and latency is lifelong. Reactivation follows stress, fever, ultraviolet light, local trauma, menstruation, immunosuppression, or waning cell-mediated immunity with age.

blocks.caption: The anatomy of latency explains why recurrences always return to the same dermatome or perioral site.

blocks.text: The site of latency therefore predicts the clinical pattern. Herpes simplex type 1, acquired through oral contact, is latent in the trigeminal ganglion, so recurrences appear as herpes labialis at the vermilion border, and less often as herpetic gingivostomatitis, herpetic whitlow on a finger, keratitis with dendritic corneal ulcers, or temporal lobe encephalitis. Herpes simplex type 2, acquired sexually, is latent in the sacral dorsal root ganglia, so recurrences are genital, perianal, or buttock lesions, with neonatal infection acquired during passage through an infected birth canal. Either type can infect either site, so distribution suggests but does not prove the type. Varicella zoster differs in that primary infection is systemic: the virus enters by the respiratory route, replicates in lymphoid tissue, and produces a viremia that seeds skin in successive waves, which is why chickenpox lesions appear in crops at different stages at once. It becomes latent in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia along the whole axis, so reactivation travels down one sensory nerve and gives the painful unilateral dermatomal eruption of zoster, often preceded by neuritic pain and sometimes followed by postherpetic neuralgia from damage to the sensory neuron.

blocks.predict: A patient with recurrent crops of vesicles on one buttock has a Tzanck smear with multinucleated giant cells. Why does this not establish whether the cause is herpes simplex or zoster, and what feature of the history would separate them?
blocks.explain: Both viruses fuse keratinocytes through envelope glycoproteins, so both give multinucleated giant cells, and the smear sees the cytopathic effect rather than the virus. Recurrence is the discriminator: herpes simplex type 2 reactivates repeatedly from sacral ganglia, while zoster typically occurs once because reactivation restores immunity, so repeated identical attacks in one site favor herpes simplex.

sections.title: Cutibacterium acnes and Pseudomonas aeruginosa: follicular infections

blocks.text: Cutibacterium acnes, formerly Propionibacterium acnes, is a gram-positive, non-spore-forming, anaerobic to aerotolerant rod that is normal flora of the sebaceous follicle. It ferments glycerol and other substrates to propionic acid and is slow growing, which is why it is also a classic cause of indolent prosthetic device and shunt infection. It is a commensal rather than an invader, and acne begins with changes in the follicle rather than with the organism. Androgens, principally dihydrotestosterone formed locally by 5-alpha-reductase, enlarge the sebaceous gland and raise sebum output, while abnormal keratinization of the follicular infundibulum with retained corneocytes plugs the duct. The result is a closed, lipid-rich, anaerobic microcomedone, which is exactly the environment the organism needs, so it multiplies there to high density.

Two activities then convert a plugged follicle into an inflammatory lesion. Bacterial lipases hydrolyze sebum triglycerides into free fatty acids, which are comedogenic and directly irritating to the follicular epithelium and which also promote further abnormal keratinization. At the same time, cell wall peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acid engage Toll-like receptor 2 on keratinocytes and infiltrating monocytes, with signaling through MyD88 and NF-kappaB and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-8, interleukin-12, and tumor necrosis factor. Interleukin-8 recruits neutrophils, whose enzymes weaken the follicular wall, and when the wall ruptures, keratin, sebum, and bacteria spill into the dermis and provoke an intense foreign body and suppurative response. That progression accounts for the clinical sequence: open and closed comedones, then inflammatory papules and pustules, then nodules and scarring where dermal rupture has occurred.

blocks.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa illustrates follicular infection from the environment rather than from flora. It is a gram-negative, non-lactose-fermenting, strictly aerobic rod, oxidase positive (which distinguishes it from the Enterobacteriaceae), motile by a single polar flagellum, and recognizable by a grape-like odor and blue-green pyocyanin and pyoverdine pigment. It needs minimal nutrients, thrives in warm water, and forms biofilms on wet surfaces, so it persists in hot tubs and whirlpools when the water is warm enough to dissipate free chlorine and chlorination is not maintained. Prolonged immersion hydrates and softens the stratum corneum and the follicular opening, and water trapped against skin by a swimsuit holds a high inoculum against follicles. The result is hot tub folliculitis: pruritic follicular papules and pustules appearing about 8 hours to 2 days after exposure, concentrated where the swimsuit held water and sparing exposed skin, and usually self-limited because infection stays within the follicle. Pyocyanin generates reactive oxygen species and, with exotoxin A and elastase, explains why the same organism destroys deeper tissue in a burn, a puncture wound, or a neutropenic patient, including the black eschar of ecthyma gangrenosum.

sections.title: Vector-borne and soil-acquired infections that present on the skin

blocks.text: When an arthropod or a larva breaches the epidermis it bypasses every surface defense and delivers organisms directly into dermis, where blood vessels, lymphatics, and tissue macrophages are waiting. The skin lesion that follows is the first and sometimes only clue to the organism, and board questions usually give a vector, a season, a geographic region, and a rash pattern. The pattern itself is mechanistic: it reflects whether the organism spreads outward through dermal connective tissue, infects endothelium, lives inside macrophages, or migrates through the epidermis as a parasite that cannot complete its life cycle.

Borrelia burgdorferi, a microaerophilic spirochete, is transmitted by the nymphal Ixodes tick, usually after about 36 to 48 hours of attachment, during which the organism changes surface proteins and migrates from the tick midgut to the salivary glands. In skin it moves outward through dermal collagen by flagellar motility and binds host plasminogen and integrins, producing erythema migrans: a slowly expanding erythematous annular lesion, often with central clearing, that is warm but typically neither painful nor pruritic and that appears about 3 to 30 days after the bite.

Rickettsia rickettsii, an obligate intracellular gram-negative organism, is transmitted by Dermacentor ticks and invades and replicates within vascular endothelial cells, spreading cell to cell by actin-based motility. The resulting vasculitis with endothelial injury, platelet consumption, and leakage explains why the rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever is macular and then petechial, begins on the wrists and ankles about 2 to 5 days after fever starts, spreads centripetally to the trunk, and characteristically involves palms and soles. The same vascular injury accounts for hyponatremia, thrombocytopenia, and the risk of shock.

Leishmania species are transmitted by the bite of a phlebotomine sandfly as promastigotes, which are phagocytosed by dermal macrophages and survive inside the phagolysosome as amastigotes; the granulomatous response to that intracellular infection produces a painless papule that enlarges into a chronic ulcer with a raised indurated border. Cutaneous larva migrans has no vector at all: larvae of the dog and cat hookworms Ancylostoma braziliense and Ancylostoma caninum, hatched in sand or soil contaminated with animal feces, penetrate bare skin directly but lack the collagenase needed to cross the basement membrane in a human host, so they wander within the epidermis and create an intensely itchy, raised, serpiginous track that advances a few millimeters to a few centimeters a day.

blocks.predict: Two febrile patients have expanding skin lesions after outdoor exposure. One has a single warm annular patch with central clearing and no palm involvement; the other has petechiae on the wrists, ankles, palms, and soles. Which organism infects endothelium, and how does the rash tell you?
blocks.explain: The second. Rickettsia rickettsii replicates in endothelial cells, so injury to vessel walls produces petechiae and involves acral skin including palms and soles, spreading centripetally. Borrelia burgdorferi stays in dermal connective tissue and spreads outward from the bite, so it gives one expanding annular lesion without petechiae or palmar involvement.

integration.text: Skin structure selects its pathogens. The cornified, lipid-rich, shedding surface explains why dermatophytes needed keratinases and why Malassezia became lipid dependent, why the sebaceous follicle supports an anaerobe, and why papillomavirus had to tie its replication cycle to keratinocyte differentiation. The same structure explains how each one is defeated: an intact barrier, so that breaks from maceration, shaving, scratching, eczema, a tick mouthpart, or a hookworm larva are the usual entry events. One step deeper, immunology decides the outcome. Opsonization and neutrophil killing contain the pyogenic cocci, which is why their virulence factors target IgG, complement, and neutrophils themselves. Th17 and interleukin-17 maintain epithelial surfaces, and neutrophils guard tissue, which is why the level at which Candida causes disease reads out the specific defect. Cytotoxic T cells control the herpesviruses and clear molluscum, so latency and encoded immune evasion are the viral answers, and waning cellular immunity with age or immunosuppression is what permits zoster and extensive molluscum.

Pathology and the laboratory then connect the organism to the finding on the slide, and this is where most exam reasoning happens. Epidermal splitting with intact mucosa means a toxin cleaving desmoglein 1, not infection of the blister itself. Multinucleated giant cells mean glycoprotein-mediated cell fusion by a herpesvirus, with the smear unable to name which one. Koilocytes mean papillomavirus replicating in differentiating cells, while cytoplasmic inclusions mean a poxvirus that never needed the nucleus. Limits are worth stating: potassium hydroxide, Tzanck smear, and Gram stain are insensitive and nonspecific, culture takes time and a dermatophyte may take weeks, colonization is not infection for Candida, Malassezia, and Cutibacterium acnes, which are normal residents, and a negative test never excludes any of these organisms. Reasoning from mechanism to finding, and acknowledging where a test cannot decide, is what the biomedical portion of the exam is testing.

summary: Staphylococcus aureus is a catalase and coagulase positive gram-positive cluster; coagulase walls off abscesses, protein A blocks opsonization by binding IgG Fc, and Panton-Valentine leukocidin lyses neutrophils.

Exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1 for a superficial, mucosa-sparing epidermal split, and TSST-1 is a superantigen; mecA-encoded PBP2a resists beta-lactams by having a low-affinity target, not by destroying the drug.
Streptococcus pyogenes is catalase negative, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, and PYR positive; M protein binds factor H and streptokinase dissolves fibrin, so it spreads rather than walls off.
Skin strains of group A strep cause immune complex glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever, which requires molecular mimicry by rheumatogenic throat M types.

Dermatophytes use keratinases to live in dead keratin and show branching septate hyphae on potassium hydroxide; Trichophyton takes skin, hair, and nail, Microsporum spares nail, Epidermophyton spares hair.
Malassezia is a lipid-dependent yeast giving spaghetti and meatballs on potassium hydroxide, with hypopigmentation from azelaic acid inhibition of tyrosinase.

Candida albicans forms budding yeast with pseudohyphae and is germ tube positive at 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 degrees Fahrenheit); Th17 and IL-17 defects give mucocutaneous disease while neutropenia allows invasion.

High-risk HPV integrates, disrupts E2, and lets E6 degrade p53 and E7 release E2F from Rb; koilocytes mark nuclear replication, while molluscum poxvirus replicates in cytoplasm and leaves molluscum bodies.
HSV-1 is latent in the trigeminal ganglion, HSV-2 in sacral ganglia, and varicella zoster in dorsal root and cranial ganglia; Tzanck multinucleated giant cells cannot separate them.

Acne starts with androgen-driven sebum and a follicular plug that lets Cutibacterium acnes release free fatty acids and trigger TLR2 inflammation, while erythema migrans, an acral-to-central petechial rash with palms and soles, a chronic ulcer with a raised border, and a moving serpiginous track point to Borrelia, Rickettsia rickettsii, Leishmania, and hookworm larvae.

verify: Nasal carriage rates for Staphylococcus aureus are quoted from about 20% to 40% depending on the population studied; this chapter uses about 30%.
The proportion of T cells activated by a superantigen is given as up to about 20% in most texts; confirm the figure NABNE expects if it is tested.
The dermatophyte table (Epidermophyton sparing hair, Microsporum sparing nail) is standard review teaching, but individual species vary and some references report occasional exceptions.

Attribution of tinea versicolor hypopigmentation to azelaic acid inhibition of tyrosinase is the conventional explanation; the mechanism of hyperpigmented lesions is less settled and is described here as thickened keratin, larger melanosomes, and inflammation.

The explanation for why skin strains of group A Streptococcus do not cause rheumatic fever (M type difference plus the systemic response generated by pharyngeal lymphoid tissue) is the prevailing model rather than a settled fact; confirm the depth NABNE expects.

Minimum Ixodes attachment time for Borrelia transmission is commonly given as about 36 to 48 hours, with shorter times reported; the interval to erythema migrans (about 3 to 30 days) also varies by source.
Onset interval for hot tub folliculitis is quoted from about 8 hours to several days; this chapter uses about 8 hours to 2 days.
Candidalysin and the CARD9 and dectin-1 pathway are current mycology and immunology consensus but are newer than many board review sources; confirm whether this level of detail is expected.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the current genus name Cutibacterium acnes, the former Propionibacterium acnes, or both.
